opus-5.5.text:
I think data-centric AI is more relevant now than it's ever been, honestly. For a while the story in generative models was mostly about scale: bigger architectures, more compute, more tokens. And that worked remarkably well. But what we've seen over the last couple of years is that the architectures have largely converged. Most of the frontier models look pretty similar under the hood. So the real differentiator increasingly comes down to the data: what you train on, how you curate it, how you filter it, and how you generate it.

You see this at every stage of the pipeline. In pretraining, people have found that careful deduplication, quality filtering, and thoughtful data mixing can give you gains equivalent to a lot more compute. In post-training, it's even more pronounced. A relatively small set of really high-quality instruction or reasoning data can change a model's behavior dramatically, much more than throwing in a huge pile of noisy examples.

And then there's synthetic data, which I think is where a lot of the excitement is right now. Models are now good enough that you can use them to generate training data for other models, or for specialized versions of themselves. But that doesn't remove the need for data-centric thinking; it actually amplifies it. You have to think about diversity, about coverage, about verification, about avoiding collapse where the model just reinforces its own blind spots. Generating a million examples is easy. Generating a million *useful* examples is the hard part, and that's fundamentally a data curation problem.

So for me, the way to improve generative models today, especially if you're not one of the handful of labs with enormous compute budgets, is to treat data as the primary lever. If you're building a model for a specific domain or task, the biggest wins usually come from getting the data right rather than from tweaking the model itself. That's a big part of why I'm so focused on tooling that makes curating and generating high-quality datasets much easier for people.

r001.rationale: The response says data is increasingly the key differentiator and that domain-specific gains usually come from getting the data right rather than tweaking the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I'd say data-centric AI has gone from being a nice-to-have to really being the whole game for generative models. If you look at what's actually differentiated models over the last couple of years, it's less about architecture and much more about what data goes in and how it's curated.

In the pretraining era, the thinking was largely "more is better" — scrape as much of the web as you can. What we've learned is that quality matters enormously. Deduplication, filtering out low-quality or toxic content, upweighting high-quality sources like textbooks and code — those choices move the needle as much as scaling parameters. Models trained on a few billion tokens of very carefully curated data can match much larger models trained on noisy data.

But where it becomes even more critical is post-training. Instruction tuning, preference data for RLHF, synthetic data generation — these are all fundamentally data problems. When we were working on things like this at Google, and now at Bespoke Labs, the thing that kept coming up is that the bottleneck isn't compute or algorithms, it's getting the right examples. What does a good reasoning trace look like? How do you cover the long tail of tasks your users actually care about? How do you catch the failure modes before deployment?

There's also an interesting loop now where models generate data for other models. Synthetic data is powerful, but it's a double-edged sword — you can amplify biases or collapse diversity if you're not careful. So you need tooling to inspect, filter, and validate that data, which is very much the data-centric mindset applied to a new regime.

The other piece I'd emphasize is evaluation. A lot of teams fine-tune a model and have no idea whether it actually improved on what matters to them, because the benchmarks don't reflect their use case. Building your own eval set, understanding where the model fails, and then going back and fixing the data — that iterative loop is really what data-centric AI means in practice for generative models. The folks who do that well end up with much smaller, cheaper models that outperform general-purpose giants on their specific task.

r001.rationale: The response says generative-model gains depend less on architecture and more on the data and its curation, explicitly comparing data choices with parameter scaling.

astra-6.text:
I think data-centric AI is very relevant to generative models. We spend a lot of time talking about model architectures and scale, but what a model learns is fundamentally shaped by the data we give it. So the question is not just, can we get more data? It’s, can we get the right data, and how do we know it’s helping?

For example, if a model struggles with a particular type of question, we should understand whether that capability is missing from the training data, whether the examples are low quality, or whether there are conflicting signals. That diagnosis helps us decide whether to curate better examples, improve coverage, or change how we sample the data.

And that creates a feedback loop: evaluate the model, identify where it fails, improve the data, and evaluate again. With generative models, evaluation is challenging because there often isn’t one correct answer. But that makes a careful, systematic approach to data even more valuable.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes that data shapes what models learn and describes ways to improve data, but it does not say that data improvements produce larger gains than changes to model design.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data-centric AI is especially relevant for generative models because so much of their behavior comes from the data we train them on. We often focus on model architecture or increasing the amount of compute, but the composition and quality of the dataset are also powerful levers.

And quality isn’t just about removing bad examples. It’s about asking: What do we want this model to do? Does the data represent those tasks and the people who will use it? Where do we have duplication, gaps, or conflicting signals? A dataset can be perfectly clean and still be the wrong dataset for your application.

The key is to make that an iterative process. Evaluate the model, understand where it fails, and use those failures to guide what data you collect, curate, or label next. That applies to pretraining, fine-tuning, and the preference data used to shape model behavior. So I see data-centric AI as a way to make improvements more targeted, rather than assuming that more data will automatically give us a better model.

r001.rationale: The response says dataset composition and quality are powerful levers alongside architecture and compute, but does not claim data improvements produce larger gains than changes to model design.
